lesson.title: Power at an Instant: Why AC Power Isn't Constant
lesson.summary: Instantaneous power in an AC circuit oscillates at twice the source frequency around a constant average, and separating those two pieces is the key to understanding real AC power.
lesson.body:
In a DC circuit, power delivered to a resistor is a single number, P = VI, because voltage and current never change. In an AC circuit, voltage and current are both changing every instant, so the power delivered changes every instant too; this is instantaneous power, p(t) = v(t)i(t). Unlike voltage or current alone, it is not itself a simple sinusoid: it oscillates at twice the original frequency and spends part of its cycle above its average and part below, sometimes even going negative when energy flows backward into the source.

For a sinusoidal voltage v(t) = Vm cos(ωt) driving a current i(t) = Im cos(ωt − θ), where θ is the phase angle by which current lags voltage, the instantaneous power is their product: p(t) = Vm Im cos(ωt) cos(ωt − θ). Using the trigonometric product-to-sum identity, this expands to p(t) = (VmIm/2)[cos θ + cos(2ωt − θ)]. The first term is constant in time; it does not depend on t at all. The second term oscillates at 2ω, twice the frequency of the original voltage and current.

Using the series RL circuit's peak values, Vm = 170 V and Im = 3.39 A, the peak of the 2.4 A rms current found from Z = 50∠53.13° Ω, with θ = 53.13°: p(t) = (170 × 3.39/2)[cos 53.13° + cos(2×377t − 53.13°)] = 288.2[0.6000 + cos(754t − 53.13°)] = 172.9 + 288.2 cos(754t − 53.13°) W. At t = 0, p(0) = 172.9 + 288.2 cos(−53.13°) = 172.9 + 288.2(0.6000) = 172.9 + 172.9 = 345.8 W. Checking directly: v(0) = 170 cos(0) = 170 V, i(0) = 3.39 cos(−53.13°) = 3.39(0.6000) = 2.034 A, so p(0) = 170 × 2.034 = 345.8 W, confirming the expanded formula.

The constant term, (VmIm/2) cos θ, is the average power actually delivered to the circuit over a full cycle, since the oscillating cos(2ωt − θ) term contributes zero net energy when averaged over time; it simply shuttles energy back and forth without a net transfer. That constant term is exactly what average power, the next section, formalizes using rms values instead of peak values, producing the compact and far more commonly used formula P = Vrms Irms cos θ.

Decomposing p(t) further separates it into two physically distinct pieces tied to the two different circuit elements doing the work. The resistor's instantaneous power, i(t)²R, is always greater than or equal to zero, since it depends on current squared, so the resistor is always either dissipating energy or momentarily doing nothing, never returning energy to the source. The inductor's instantaneous power swings symmetrically positive and negative, since it alternately stores energy in its magnetic field and releases that same energy back into the circuit; averaged over a full cycle, the inductor's contribution is exactly zero. This is the physical origin of the split between average power, tied to resistance, and reactive power, tied to reactance, formalized in the next two sections.
